newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE-Life gets tougher for Kabul street children.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Life gets tougher for Kabul street children.

text.p: Destitute children struggling for a livelihood on the streets of war-shattered Kabul are finding life harder as their numbers multiply, aid workers say.

"With the lack of jobs and the burden of displaced families from north of Kabul, the situation is getting worse for street children," said Yousaf, the director of Aashiyana, a Swiss-based charity which provides basic education, hygiene and vocational classes for nearly 600 street children.

The International Committee of the Red Cross estimates that 60,000 people have sought refuge in Kabul from fighting north of the capital in recent months. The ruling Taleban militia has not allowed them to return to their homes in the Shomali Valley.

A survey conducted by Aashiyana last year estimated that 28,000 children were working the streets of the Afghan capital, but since then economic hardship has forced many more families to send their children out to earn what they can.
"There are now 50,000 to 60,000 street children in Kabul and the number is increasing," said Yousaf. "They need to work to find food for their families, but opportunities are few."

The children, many of whom have lost at least one parent in the violence convulsing Afghanistan, polish shoes, wash cars and scavenge for twigs or paper that can be burned as fuel. Some also beg when they get desperate at the end of the day.
HOPE AND SUPPORT -- FOR A FEW
Those who find their way to the Aashiyana centre can get one meal a day and classes that teach literacy as well as skills such as embroidery, tailoring and making artificial flowers.
The centre is the only place in Kabul where girls can learn to read or write -- the purist Islamic Taleban militia barred girls from education when they captured the city in September.
The Taleban also excluded most women from the workplace, imposing severe economic hardship on the many families headed by women or dependent on the wages of women wage-earners.

Nooriya, an eight-year-old girl collects paper and branches to sell for cooking fuel and some day she begs, earning no more than 5,000 Afghanis ($0.20) a day. Her father was killed in a rocket attack five years ago and her mother can no longer work.
"My mother was doing some laundry job but she is too weak now," says Nooriya. "My elder sister is 16 and my mother does not think it appropriate for her to work outside the house."
Nooriya is among the children under Aashiyana's wing, but aid workers face constant reminders of the plight of others.
"I was monitoring lunch distribution one day when a girl refused to eat, saying she ought to take the food home to her little sister who had not eaten for two days," said Yousaf.
Ghaffar, a doctor in charge of an Afghan charity called International Orphan Care, said some mothers could not cope with the strain of seeing their children in dire straits.
"One woman desperate for food and medicine for her five ill children tried to commit suicide, but fortunately her neighbour found her. She was taken to hospital and she recovered," he said.
TALEBAN RULES TOUGH ON WOMEN
Ghaffar established his centre for orphans in 1994, but also feeds single mothers who come for one meal a day.
Aadila, who used to work as a seamstress, said Taleban restrictions had made life hard for women.

"At least in the past women were able to work as labourers or employees in government or foreign aid agency offices. But with the Taleban's ban on women working outside the home, except in the medical sector, life is getting more difficult for us," she said, waiting for lunch.

Aadila's all-enveloping burqa was soaked in sweat as she waited in the heat, with her children squeezed under her robe to shelter from the sun. "Life could be worse," she told them as they clamoured to know when the food would be served.
Like most of the women who come to the centre, Aadila is a widow -- Kabul has an estimated 60,000 widows among its one million people, most of them with children to support.
To ensure that her five children survive, Aadila begs for money or collects scraps from restaurants.
She walks five km (three miles) to Ghaffar's centre for the daily meal of beans and rice. At home they live mostly on bread and tea, the staple diet for many impoverished Kabulis.
"I can't help all of them," said Ghaffar ruefully.
He urged foreign relief agencies to focus more on teaching people useful skills or organising food-for-work programmes and less on subsidising bakeries or providing hand-outs.

"Foreign agencies have trained Afghans as beggars. We require vocational programmes for our people so they can earn something and stand on their own feet," Ghaffar said. "That way people won't become lazy and won't be dependent in the future."
